Durham Mining Museum - Newspaper Articles

 17 th December 1938, Page: 187, Column: 1

## Review Of Coal Mining Industry

 By George Raw, B.Sc., M.Inst.C.E., M.I.M.E. 

 From presidential address before the North of England Institute of Mining and Mechanical Engineers. 

 The nation's coalfields resemble a colliery in that the management may estimate the coal remaining to be worked, and dividing that by the current annual production, conclude that the colliery has a lifetime of a certain number of years. Such a forecast, however, cannot mature in practice. The better seams become exhausted, the less economic ones remain, and those less economic seams become still more uneconomic as the workings extend. 

 25 Years' Progress. 

 In 1913 only 8 per cent. of the coal was produced hy the use of coal-cutting machines, but in 1937 that proportion was 57 per cent. As recently as 1928 only 12 per cent. of the output was mechanically conveyed below ground. In 1937 the proportion was 51 per cent. 

 In the year 1913 again 287,430,473 tons of saleable coal were produced by 1,104,406 employees. In the year 1937, 240,409,436 tons were produced by 802,084 employees. The production per employee in 1913 was 260 tons, while the production per employee in 1937 was 300 tons, an increase of 15 per cent. from coal mines which did not possess on the average such favourable mining conditions as in 1913. 

 However satisfactory productivity may be, it must be related to (1) Safety (2) The miners' earnings relative to the cost of living ; and (3) The cost of production. 

 In 1913, the fatal accident rate per million tons of coal produced was 4.61 due to all causes other than explosions. In 1937, the fatal accident rate on the same basis had fallen to 331. 

 In 1913 the fatal accident rate from all causes other than explosions was 1.20 per 1,000 employees. In 1937, the fatality rate on the same basis was 0.99. 

 It would appear that the average earnings of employees in British coal mines in the month of June 1914 was 6s. 10d. per shift worked, the cost of living being then regarded as representing 100 units. In 1937 the average earnings were 11s. 0.78d. per shift, the cost of living index being 155 units. The remuneration, therefore, of the miners, expressed in terms of the cost of living. was 4¼ per cent. higher in 1937 than in 1914, the miners' hours below ground in that interval having been reduced from 8 to 7½. 

 Figures for 1913 show that the average cost at the pithead per ton of commercially disposable coal was 8s. 7½d. compared with 14s. 7.77d. in the year 1937. 

 The quarter of a century's progress, therefore, may be summed up by the statement that under deteriorating coal seam conditions (1) The production per employee has increased by 15 per cent.; (2) The fatality rate per million tons of coal produced, for accidents other than explosions, has fallen by 28 per cent. and by 17½ per cent, on the same basis per 1,000 employees; (3) Miners' earnings have risen relatively to the cost of living by 4½ per cent. ; and (4) The cost of production has increased by 70 per cent. in terms of monetary values. 

 Disquieting Feature. 

 If this monetary production cost increase of 70 per cent. be discounted by the rise in commodity values, the cost of production may be represented as an approximate increase of 9½ per cent. between the years 1913 and 1937, expressed in terms of commodity values. The year 1937 has been deliberately compared with the year 1913 for the good reason that the two years were comparable from the standpoint of industrial prosperity. 

 Whatever value may attach to this resume as a basis of prophecy for the future, it justifies the claim that Britain merits the place she holds in the vanguard of the world's coal mining practice. The increase in the cost of production between 1913 and 1937 of 9½ per cent. on comparable terms of commodity values is largely accounted for by the miners' reduced hours, by the greater reject due to better coal cleaning, and by the 4¼ per cent. net increase in the miners' earnings. 

 Had the hours of work been the same in 1937 as in 1913, and had the 1937 wages been no greater in commodity value than in 1913, the cost of production expressed in terms of commodity values would probably have been approximately equal in 1937 to that of 1913. The gravely disquieting feature, however, is the fact that while the production of coal by mechanical coal-cutting rose from 8 per cent. to 57 per cent. between 1913 and 1937, the cost reduction effect of this great increase in mechanical production was negatived by other factors of which the principal is probably that of the less economic character of the coal seams now being worked. 

 The cancellation by other factors of the cost reduction effect upon the production of coal represented by an increase in coal-cutting of 49 per cent. in 25 years and an increase in mechanical conveying of 39 per cent. in 9 years, is a condition of affairs to which grave thought must be given. 

 It may be suggested that there is a remaining margin of economy available in the 43 per cent. of coal now being produced by other means than coal-cutting, and that 49 per cent. of the coal produced continues as yet to be transported by other means than mechanical conveyors. But the superficial value of these figures must be discounted, The 43 per cent. of coal produced otherwise than by coal-cutting largely represents the more easily won coal seams in the working of which mechanical cutting exhibits little, if any, advantage. Large numbers of pneumatic picks are in use also, the production from which is not included in the figure of 57 per cent, representing the machine-cut coal produced in 1937. 

 One further reason may be proposed for the failure of the 49 per cent. increase of mechanisation to reduce production costs on a commodity value basis during the past 25 years, and that is the restrictive effect of the Marketing Schemes operating under the Coal Mines Act, 1930. Why, it may be urged, should the older and less economic collieries not be closed, and the newer collieries permitted to produce more of the coal required. A substantial reduction in the nation's pithead costs, it is urged, would then be secured, Among the numerous objections to such a course are the following : (1) Each of the great industrial regions in the country has built up its industry on the basis not only of a plentiful supply of coal from its adjacent coalfield at relatively low transport charges, but on the basis also of the particular type of coal which that coalfield provided, 

 (2) Valuable coal reserves would be abandoned and probably lost for all time, 

 (3) The solution could only be temporary, for the newer collieries would in turn grow older, 

 (4) New "Special Areas" would be created in the older coalfields, 

 If the mining industry is to maintain social progress commensurate with that of other industries, facing as it must do deteriorating underground conditions, an increase in production costs during the next 25 years of 20 per cent. or 30 per cent. must be anticipated, unless adequate cost increase prevention measures can be found. 

 Necessity for Cost Consciousness. 

 To combat the effect of deteriorating underground conditions on the future cost of production, efforts must be made to develop (1) A wider production cost consciousness, and (2) Continued scientific improvement in coal mining technique. 

 The industry must provide (1) The maximum of safety; (2) The national social standards for the miners ; and (3) A sufficient margin of profit to attract into and retain the necessary capital in the industry with which to maintain efficiency and continued expenditure on costly modern plant. 

 Whatever results may be anticipated from amalgamation of existing units into larger groups, the coal owners and their managements must be able to rely on a more general and more definite coal production cost consciousness on the part of all members and associates of the industry, including statutory authorities in London and elsewhere, Too much relief must not be anticipated from scientific progress. 

 Further improvement in mining technique will doubtless take place, but faced as the industry is with increasingly expensive underground conditions, a much greater general appreciation of the importance of economy in the cost of coal production is, in the national interests, of equal or possibly even greater importance than improved mining machinery. 

 There is an old proverb ascribed to Thos. Fuller: "To see may be easy, but to foresee — that is the fine thing." Such a capacity becomes increasingly necessary as the years pass — a capacity to assess an industry's future problems — a capacity to prepare in anticipation a solution of those problems.
